title: Ankit Goyal - Infrastructure for Long Running Agents

segments.text: ANKIT GOYAL: Good afternoon, everyone.
I'm Ankit.
I'm a principal staff engineer at LinkedIn in the AI platforms
team.
I'm going to give an overview of our agentic platform
and talk about some of the trends
we are observing as we scale agent-driven experimentation.
So first, I'd like to introduce some of the agents
that we are running in production
and that have delivered significant business value.
So first is model generation.
So LinkedIn runs 400-plus models in production that are written
in TensorFlow.
And we are trying to migrate them to PyTorch.
Now, we have written an agentic workflow that can do that.
And the challenging part in this agent
is ensuring that the new models that we are generating,
they perform either on par or better than the production
deployed models.
And those production deployment models usually
have been human-tuned by engineers over multiple months
or even years.
The next is performance-optimization agent.
So this is an agent that we run in our cluster that
looks for low-utilization jobs.
It basically profiles them, benchmarks them.
We have a whole knowledge base that our team has collected
over the years, and it optimizes them and creates a pull request
for different teams to review.
And then finally, to build on top of that,
we have an autonomous research agent
where engineers can define an objective,
and this agent will autonomously do architectural sweeps
or hyperparameter tunings to basically optimize
for the objective.
Now, all these agents have a fundamental life cycle
that they share.
The first one is an engineer writes a hypothesis,
writes an objective.
And the agent then forms an hypothesis.
It generates the code, runs it on our GPUs, and then the agent
evaluates the outcome.
Now, this loop can run over hours or even days continuously,
autonomously, without human intervention.
Now, with introduction of agents into the infrastructure,
we observe certain shifts in how to architecture
the infrastructure.
One is the UX.
Traditionally, we focused a lot on creating rich abstractions
so that engineers can write their machine learning pipelines
or their training loops easily, or how to access data.
Those are still important, but that code today
is now generated by LLMs.
So the focus of our users have shifted
towards creating agentic workflows
and creating appropriate guardrails so that agents don't
deviate from the original task.
The other is compute.
Engineers typically launched a limited number
of long-running jobs in our cluster.
A couple of minutes of delay was usually
amortized over the run of the training job.
Agents, however, can launch hundreds of jobs
within a very short period of time,
and ranging from a few minutes to hours to even days.
And finally, the trust.
We inherently trust the code written by humans or engineers.
However, agent-generated code needs
to run in a very constrained environment.
So to support this in our infrastructure,
agent is just like any other task.
Users write agents as if they're writing any other PyTorch
or TensorFlow job.
The difference is, the agent code is untrusted.
So it runs in a highly restricted environment,
like no egress, no access to credentials,
and all the communication goes via our proxies
using the agent's own identity.
Now natural-language prompts they
tend to not do well when agents are running
for long periods of time.
So we follow harness-as-code approach for all our agents.
Each stage is defined in code and has
its own responsibilities.
And additionally, and more importantly,
the scorer and evaluators are also defined in code,
so that agents don't do reward hacking
or they don't diverge from the path.
And then we have a whole ecosystem of tasks,
memory management, and how do agents share their learnings
with other agents of the same type, different type,
and then the notifications for human-in-the-loop-type
of interactions.
Now, given these agents can run over long periods of time,
we also have a robust checkpointing
and restore, so that agents can autonomously
recover from any failures without any human interventions.
Now, as I mentioned, these agents
can launch very large number of jobs.
And this creates a bottleneck in our control
plane, which has been designed with a lot of abstraction.
And those abstractions add up once agents
start launching a lot of jobs.
So we have built a customized control plane, which
maintains a warm pool of GPU pods,
and it can provide a very low-latency job launch.
Similarly, since we are running agent-generated code,
this pool of pods is highly restricted,
with no egress, read-only access to data,
and it runs in a highly unprivileged mode.
So the impact of agents is clear.
The number of experiments in our cluster
has grown by 100% over the last six months.
We are continuously investing in our evaluations
so that our experiments can turn to real production value.
Additionally, we are investing in SLMs for specialized tasks.
And we're also looking into GPU-sharing techniques,
so that we can get more utilization out of our GPUs
as they keep getting bigger, but not all the tasks
are bigger to utilize the full GPU.
So the goal with the agents, for us,
is to take more shots at the goal.
The more shots at the goal we take,
the more improvements we can make to our models,
and eventually improving the member experience
and providing more business value.
So thank you.
